articles.title_orig: France shuts down nearly 900 schools as violent education protests escalate
articles.title_zh: France shuts down nearly 900 schools as violent education protests escalate
articles.content_orig:
France is struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades. What started as a demonstration in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school to the north of Paris has snowballed into a national crisis.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close and more than 6,000 people have been taken into police custody over the past few weeks, most of them minors with no previous criminal records. Students, teachers and policemen have been injured. One student in the north-east city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade and another in Tours, the use of an eye.
Authorities estimate hundreds of thousands of protesters, including students, teachers and delegates from trade unions, took to the streets on Tuesday as protests sweep the country.
In Paris, tear gas filled the air, and trash cans, school desks and chairs were set alight as riot police with shields and batons clashed with some demonstrators.
The original protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on September 21 attracted little attention. Pupils had joined their teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff sent to the school, the strike ended, but by then the match had been lit. According to student leader Manès Nadel, it spread like wildfire.
“It’s an unprecedented number of schools that are now involved,” he said, adding that France’s Education Ministry had been “totally overwhelmed by the crisis.”
Despite their suburban beginnings, the protests are now drawing international attention. US President Donald Trump claimed Tuesday that “what’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration.”
“This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
Pupils at lycées in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances, and within days similar scenes were reported across the country, from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement. More than 100 high schools have been damaged since the start of the protest movement.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. One policeman was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in Alençon, a technique now prohibited by law.
The violence and the speed with which the protests have grown have taken many by surprise, but the grievances are long-standing — an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system that many students feel is no longer fit for purpose. Videos have circulated for years showing classrooms with too few desks or chairs, or students finding their classes cancelled when an absent teacher is not replaced.
A fertility spike in France in 2010 has led to a rise in the number of high school students now attending schools that have seen years of real-terms funding cuts. Secondary schools now have fewer teachers than in 2008, despite an extra 250,000 students enrolled. In the public sector, 70% of classrooms have more than 30 pupils per class.
Critics say the government’s response has been slow and tin-eared. Initially much of it was focused on the far-left LFI party and its presence at the barricades. The party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, who’s expected to do well in the country’s presidential election next spring, has repeatedly defended both the students’ right to protest and his party’s right to be there. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for a firm police response and the cost of the protest. Damage to schools in the greater Paris region alone is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.84 million).
There was an initial concession over the fees at technological high schools that had been planned for 2027 but this has now been removed from the government’s budget. “The government’s response has been irresponsible and it confirms exactly why the students are angry, because they are never heard,” said Manes. “They are responding only with repression.”
The protesters do now have the government’s full attention, especially after a spike in violence late last week, when the interior minister noted a shift from student protest to urban violence and some 2,000 people were taken into custody in a single day. On Friday, Edouard Geffray, the education minister, met with student leaders. No agreement was reached, however, and the student leaders called for a massive turnout on Tuesday immediately afterward.
France’s interior ministry estimated there were about 256,000 protesters out on the streets nationwide on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris. Meanwhile, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, one of the high school student unions involved in organizing the demonstrations, suggested a much larger turnout of 450,000 people across the country.
More than 400 people were detained in Tuesday’s protests, the ministry said.
Some students have called for fresh demonstrations on Thursday.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, speaking in the National Assembly on Tuesday, said “extreme violence has reached the gates of our high schools and it must be condemned unequivocally.”
Lecornu said 215 students and 85 education staff have been injured during the unrest, calling it “the highest number of education staff injured in decades.” He rejected accusations that the government had ordered police to repress the protests.
He also said officials must listen to the concerns and demands of students at each school.
“That is why time will be set aside starting this week, from Wednesday, to allow each leadership team to organize a session of internal democracy within its high school,” he wrote on X.
The Education Ministry has launched an online portal where students can share their concerns and ideas for improving their education.
The government’s response is being hampered by the poor state of the public finances. It is trying to pass a 2027 budget that narrows the deficit to around 5 percent of GDP, a feat that can only be achieved by painful belt-tightening. Last week France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5 percent last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook.
The unrest has fired the starting gun on what promises to be a vicious race between the far right and far left for the presidency, with much of the center floundering in the polls. For the far left, the pupils are a natural constituency. For the government, they’re a source of disorder and of spending pressure at the worst possible moment.
Historically, student protests have not gone well for French governments. The student protest of May 1968 turned into the largest strike in French history, in a country that knows a thing or two about strikes. One of its slogans was “be realistic, ask for the impossible.”
The difference now is that the students who’ve taken to the barricades once again don’t feel they are asking for much. In fact, they say they are demanding the bare minimum: an education system that allows them to learn.
CNN’s Saskya Vandoorne, Lucie Lepellec, Kate Irby and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Privacy regulator launches probe into China-based company behind Kmart ‘pervert glasses’ app
articles.title_zh: Privacy regulator launches probe into China-based company behind Kmart ‘pervert glasses’ app
articles.content_orig:
Commissioner said Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the smartglasses, failed to respond to her inquiries
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
The Australian privacy regulator has opened an investigation into the China-based software company behind the HeyCyan app in Kmart’s $89 smartglasses, following public outrage over the covert use of the devices.
In August, Guardian Australia reported Kmart had sold out of the Anko-branded discount version of Meta’s smartglasses that can capture images and record high-definition video, which led to widespread concern and calls to ban or restrict their use.
A GetUp petition has had more than 55,000 signatures calling to restrict the use of what has been labelled as “pervert glasses”, and councils around the country have looked to ban the glasses in public spaces such as swimming pools. The federal government is also considering a restriction on use in government workplaces.
The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, was asked by the attorney general to assess the privacy implications of the glasses at the time.
Kind wrote to Kmart and BDI Technology, retailers for the glasses, as well as Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the glasses. She also wrote to Meta – for its Ray-Bans glasses – and Google which is planning its own smartglasses.
In a blog post on Wednesday , Kind announced an investigation has been opened into Shenzhen Qingcheng after it failed to respond to inquiries, “as well as concerns arising from third party analysis of the technology itself as well as the entity’s privacy policy”
None of the other companies will be investigated as part of this process, Kind said.
The privacy commissioner also highlighted the difficulty in applying privacy law to individuals who may use the devices given the privacy act only applies to companies and Commonwealth agencies – not individuals.
“Retailers that sell smart glasses – for example on an e-commerce website – or companies that manufacture them, may not have any Privacy Act obligations if they do not collect any personal information with respect to those devices,” Kind said.
“Instead, the entity providing the software at use in the device is likely to be the entity that collects and holds the information for the purpose of privacy law.”
Kind said that potential changes to the privacy act proposed by the government would strengthen how privacy law would apply to surveillance wearables such as smartglasses.
“The most substantial change will be the replacement of the ‘reasonably necessary for an entity’s functions and activities’ test with a ‘fair and reasonable’ test,” she said.
after newsletter promotion
“The new test will require an entity to look at a range of factors, including the extent to which an individual had genuine choice in the collection of their personal information, as well as the best interests of the child where children are involved.”
Kind said she hoped the community would “find comfort” in the proposed reforms as it would raise the bar over what personal information smartglasses can collect.
“These reforms are likely to become increasingly necessary as we face subsequent generations of surveillance wearables and connected devices, from personal assistant gadgets to ambient recording badges.”
Researchers at the University of Sydney in August analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”.
In a subset of these videos, about 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage.
Canterbury-Bankstown and Sydney City are among the councils in Sydney to have banned the glasses from some venues, as well as Brisbane in Queensland, and Yarra city council in Melbourne.
Shenzhen Qingcheng was approached for comment.

articles.title_orig: Germany arrests former intelligence chief in espionage case
articles.title_zh: Germany arrests former intelligence chief in espionage case
articles.content_orig:
August Hanning, the former president of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), appears as a witness before the NSA investigative committee at the German parliament Bundestag in Berlin on Oct. 1, 2015. Michael Kappeler/DPA via AP hide caption
BERLIN — A former head of Germany 's foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor's office said.
August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is "strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage," the federal prosecutor's office said in a statement.
Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D., was also arrested Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
"In one instance, there is suspicion that Mr. Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service," Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the federal prosecutor's office, told German broadcaster RTL later on Tuesday.
"In another instance, he is alleged to have passed on information following an extensive exchange — also with an employee of another intelligence service."
Neither Peterson nor the earlier statement by the prosecutor's office revealed who exactly the two men were suspected of spying for or which foreign intelligence services they provided with classified information.
Premises belonging to both men were searched Tuesday.
The prosecutor's office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning's chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.
"In his role, he had access to confidential information," the prosecutor's office said.
Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said.
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings," the statement said.
Hanning used the information in private consulting work and Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information until June 2022, Peterson said.
Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block's children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years.
The investigation into that case led to Tuesday's arrests.
The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning's residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor's office stated.
Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from Block in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor's office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa.
The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain Block House. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court.
A message to the BND for comment was not immediately returned.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
"This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story," said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
"We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations leveled against former BND chief Hanning," he told Spiegel Online.
"We have been criticizing the dubious and wide-ranging lobbying activities of former top officials and those with the highest security clearances in Germany for years," he said and called for banning former officials with security clearances from engaging in private consulting work after leaving office, Spiegel Online reported.

articles.title_orig: U.S. resident charged with helping Canadian school shooter in rampage that killed 8 in Tumbler Ridge
articles.title_zh: U.S. resident charged with helping Canadian school shooter in rampage that killed 8 in Tumbler Ridge
articles.content_orig:
An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that US defence secretary Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Parnell said the secretary of the US Army would set the time and place of the execution.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Watch: Why is America running out of execution drugs? , external
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.
Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.
The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 Hits New Record High
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 Hits New Record High
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 rose to an all-time intraday on Tuesday, touching 7844.52 and surpassing its August 13 intraday peak when it hit 7,830. The benchmark also closed for the first time over 7,800.
The recovery comes after months of oil shocks, rising borrowing costs and the possible start of a Federal Reserve rate hiking cycle.
The record rally comes just a day after the 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5.3%, reaching levels not seen since 2002. In mid September, the Fed raised its benchmark rate for the first time in over three years and indicated more were to come.
Oil had crossed $100 a barrel in early March for the first time since 2022 as the Iran conflict disrupted energy supplies moving through the Strait of Hormuz. After falling below $70 a barrel, it slingshot back above $100 in early September.
"At the end of the day, oil and bond yields can be correlated, but so is the stock market and profits. And if the profits are there, which they have been, the stock market is going to be resilient, even if the economy is a bit more mixed," Shawn Snyder, economic strategist at Potomac Fund Management, told CNBC.
Unlike prior records this year, this latest run has been narrowly lead by a few stocks tied to the AI hype and deemed unfettered by adverse macroeconomic headwinds.
"When traders take a breather from the noise surrounding them — much of it negative in recent months — and look closer at what's happening in the markets, it becomes clear the U.S. stock market is the best place to park their money compared with other locations. It's hard to argue against the mostly positive risk-reward ratio we've seen over multiple decades," said JJ Kinahan, Cboe Global Markets senior vice president of retail and alternative investments.
The so-called Magnificent 7 namely, Nvidia , Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , Meta , Microsoft and Tesla make up more than 34% of the market cap of the S&P 500 .
"When you consider that much girth among a small handful of stocks, it's apparent how much these stocks' daily movements dictate the direction of the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, both of which are in record territory again today," Kinahan said.
With tech companies investing heavily in data centers and computing infrastructure demand for chips and equipment has gone up. Earlier this year, Amazon said it expected about $200 billion in capital expenditures across its businesses in 2026, citing opportunities including AI, chips and robotics.
Investor appetite for ambitious technology bets also became evident in June, when SpaceX raised $75 billion in the largest IPO ever and began trading on June 12. The debut became another milestone where investors continued backing growth companies despite higher energy prices and borrowing costs.
Looking ahead, however, Potomac Fund Management's Snyder cautioned that the "weakening" market breadth may last longer if inflation shows no signs of easing, or if there's no clear signal that the Federal Reserve is achieving its mandate. The central bank is slated to release its minutes from the September meeting on Wednesday.
The market "can look relatively calm, but there are still things going on underneath the surface that may not be so calm," Snyder said.
Correction: The 10-year Treasury yield on Monday surpassed 5.3% to reach highs not seen since 2002. An earlier version misstated the year.

articles.title_orig: After cordial Xi-Trump summit, could China’s US dollar pivot cause tremors?
articles.title_zh: After cordial Xi-Trump summit, could China’s US dollar pivot cause tremors?
articles.content_orig:
Beijing is building a financial safety net around the yuan while reducing exposure to US Treasuries – a strategy that could draw increasing scrutiny from Washington
As President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump talked tariffs, agricultural quotas and critical minerals at last month’s closely watched summit in Washington, an “elephant in the room” loomed over the discussion: China’s efforts to gradually diversify away from US dollar assets.
Beijing has gradually been cutting its holdings of US Treasuries while pushing to expand the yuan’s global use and developing alternative financial architecture. While these issues may not have featured in the summit’s official communique, they have not gone unnoticed by economists and investors – or by policymakers on both sides of the Pacific.
Charles Chang, a finance professor at Fudan University, said topics such as China’s holdings of US debt were likely to have been raised during the talks, although he added they were unlikely to result in a formal agreement similar to those covering trade.
“Unlike tariffs, which can be set out as part of a policy framework, sovereign debt management involves actual capital allocation and is highly sensitive, making it unlikely to be formally addressed in official statements,” Chang noted.

articles.title_orig: CNN now has a new owner. What will the future of the network be under Skydance?
articles.title_zh: CNN now has a new owner. What will the future of the network be under Skydance?
articles.content_orig:
CNN’s new owner, David Ellison, says he supports CNN’s legal action against the Trump administration over White House access, and will not interfere in the news organization’s coverage.
“We believe in editorial independence, and we will never interfere,” Ellison said, reiterating the reassurances he made while seeking to buy Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this year.
The merger between Warner and Paramount took effect on Tuesday morning, and Ellison held an employee town hall to introduce the newly combined company, named Skydance.
Ellison, the CEO of Skydance, laid out his vision for investing in films, shows and new technology.
“For the first time,” he said, “we have the studios, the franchises, the libraries, the talent and scale all under one roof to compete with anyone in the world.”
CNN anchor Anderson Cooper interviewed Ellison at the town hall and asked directly about CNN employees’ concerns about Skydance’s ownership.
In response, Ellison said, “I believe deeply in journalism,” and went on to call the work done by CBS News and CNN “a vital part of our democracy.”
While speaking about the need for fact-based news, Ellison said, “You go back to what President Obama said during the pandemic. He said a republic that can’t agree on the same set of facts can’t function, and I think he was 100% right about that.”
In the news space, “we want to actually help scale and transition the business digitally,” Ellison said.
He emphasized the importance of growing CNN’s digital operations and reaching new audiences worldwide, citing Skydance’s estimate that the combined company reaches more than 200 million streaming subscribers.
The newly formed company, he said, “can create an even bigger platform for the best journalism in the world.”
The Ellison family’s ties to President Donald Trump had fueled concerns among CNN employees about the network’s independence.
Last fall, Trump described Ellison and his father, the billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, as “friends of mine” and “big supporters of mine.” Last December, Trump said “it’s imperative that CNN be sold” to new owners.
Asked about the merger by a reporter on Tuesday afternoon, Trump said, “It’s going to be a great company. They’re terrific people, and it’s going to be a great company.”
At the Skydance town hall, Cooper asked a follow-up question about CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s First Amendment lawsuit over Trump’s recent attempt to ban the three news outlets from the White House.
Cooper asked, “Do you stand with CNN and our effort to completely restore access to covering President Trump?”
“Of course,” Ellison said.
The next hearing in the legal case is slated for Thursday morning.
Both CNN chairman and editor-in-chief Mark Thompson and CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss attended the town hall. The two news operations are operating separately for now.
“We trust Mark, we trust the team,” Ellison said while speaking about CNN.
Later on, Cooper asked about the likelihood of a tie-up between CBS and CNN in the future: “If Paramount and Warner Brothers are now cousins, and CBS News and CNN are cousins, when does somebody start to ask them to share organs?”
“It’s day one,” Ellison said.
He said he intends to bring the relevant business leaders “into the decision-making” now that the deal has taken effect.
Generally speaking, companies will start making integration decisions “within usually 120 days,” Ellison said, “but I think it’s foolish to try to say I’m going to show up with every single answer today.”

articles.title_orig: New Maryland defense shipyard gets $6.6 billion commitment and Trump visit
articles.title_zh: New Maryland defense shipyard gets $6.6 billion commitment and Trump visit
articles.content_orig:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said he was removed from the list of speakers at a White House event Tuesday at Baltimore County's Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center, where a major private investment was announced.
President Trump traveled to Tradepoint Atlantic on Tuesday to address Anduril Industries' plans for a two-million-square-foot, software-defined shipyard in Baltimore County.
The facility, known as Arsenal-2, is expected to expand America's submarine industrial base.
The State of Maryland and Baltimore County announced that the $3.7 billion private investment by Anduril is expected to create more than 3,100 permanent jobs.
Arsenal-2 will be built at Tradepoint Atlantic within the Sparrows Point complex. The project is expected to generate more than $2 billion in annual economic output, including an estimated $312 million in wages each year, according to the governor's office.
"This massive new project will deliver the largest private investment and create the most jobs in Maryland in over a decade—driving billions of dollars in economic activity that will boost Maryland families not just in Baltimore County, but throughout the state," Moore said. "With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs. We thank Anduril for choosing Maryland, and we're ready to build the future of the aerospace and defense economy together."
Moore was initially scheduled to speak at Tuesday's event alongside Trump but was removed from the program after the White House objected to his inclusion Monday.
Moore confirmed Tuesday that he would no longer attend the event after recording a debate with Republican gubernatorial candidate Dan Cox.
"If the President of the United States wants to bring the circus to town and tell me that I am not allowed to speak to the fact that we were the ones that helped bring the deal, then I will let the circus be conducted  while I go back to the people of Maryland," Moore said.
The White House told CBS News Baltimore that Moore was invited to attend the event as a guest.
"President Trump is willing to work with anyone to revitalize our manufacturing sector, which is why the White House graciously invited Governor Moore to attend today's event as a guest," a White House spokesperson stated. "It's unfortunate that the Governor is now making a multi-billion-dollar announcement about himself by throwing a tantrum over a federal initiative that will bring sorely needed jobs back to his state thanks to President Trump."
A spokesperson for the governor's office added, "Governor Moore has always said he will work with anyone when it comes to delivering for Marylanders but bow to no one when it comes to standing up for them. The Governor is proud to welcome Anduril to Baltimore County and the thousands of permanent jobs this investment is bringing to our state."
Rep. Johnny Olszewski, a former Baltimore County executive and current Maryland congressman, was among the Democratic lawmakers who chose not to attend the event after Moore was removed as a speaker, according to The Baltimore Banner.
Olszewski told The Banner in a statement that the focus should remain on the investment coming to Baltimore County.
"I proudly support all efforts to continue providing new opportunities for future generations," Olszewski said.
Baltimore County Councilman and county executive candidate Julian Jones also chose not to attend.
Moore and Trump have clashed on issues including the Francis Scott Key Bridge rebuild, redistricting, crime and immigration enforcement.
Last week, Moore told CBS News Baltimore that he would invite Trump to join him on a boat tour of the Francis Scott Key Bridge reconstruction site.
"I would love it if the president were to choose to join me at that, so he could see the unprecedented speed and unprecedented progress that's happening with this rebuild," Moore said.
CBS News Baltimore reached out to the White House for comment but has not heard back.
In 2025, Moore invited Trump to visit Maryland and participate in a public safety walk after the National Guard was deployed in Washington, D.C.
The White House responded by pointing to Baltimore's crime rate.
A White House spokesperson said, "Perhaps Gov. Moore should take a page out of the President's playbook."
At the time, the White House also said Baltimore was the fourth-most-dangerous city in the United States.
According to a U.S. News & World Report ranking, Baltimore ranked behind Memphis, Oakland and St. Louis.
In February 2026, Moore said he was singled out and excluded from a couple of bipartisan events for the nation's governors.
Moore said the president excluded him from a dinner for governors and their spouses for National Governors Association (NGA) in Washington, D.C., along with Colorado Gov. Jared Polis.
Moore, the vice chair of the NGA, attended the annual NGA meeting after he said the White House reinvited him.
"I will attend today's business meeting with my colleagues at the White House," Moore said. "But let me be abundantly clear: I will not participate in political stunts."

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
The prisoner received two doses of pentobarbital as authorities tried to put her to death on 30 September
Christa Pike, a Tennessee prisoner who survived the state’s attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said on Tuesday.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as Tennessee officials attempted to put her to death last Wednesday in a case that shocked many in America and created headlines around the world. She was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.
Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”.
“She is the only person known to have survived a complete execution attempt in the US. Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time. We continue to ask the Governor of Tennessee to commute Christa Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole,” Pike’s attorneys added.
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison on the night of 30 September.
Witnesses to the attempt to execute Pike described how they they heard she was choking and struggling for an hour after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her. In hospital, she was put on a ventilator and had been in critical condition.
Following the botched execution attempt, one of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey, called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”.
The disastrous attempt sparked widespread condemnation across the political spectrum and among advocates for banning the death penalty. Tennessee’s prison chief, Frank Strada, also resigned in the aftermath as Pike’s experience was the fifth botched execution under his leadership across two states since 2022.
Pike and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in 1995. The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder.
According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area behind the agriculture campus steam plant at the University of Tennessee on 12 January 1995. Pike cut Slemmer’s stomach and throat with a box cutter before smashing her head with a rock.
Shipp carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of Slemmer’s skull.
Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement that was included in her clemency petition.
As a child, Pike had been subject to various abuse, including multiple rapes by different men, as well as beatings by her relatives.
Pike later underwent nearly 30 years of solitary confinement while on death row.
In the wake of the botched execution attempt Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun who is perhaps the best-known advocate for abolition of the death penalty in America, told the Guardian : “This is the essence of cruelty. Take a conscious, imaginative human being, give her a date for her death, have her anticipate it over and over again, and then take her out and try and kill her.
“She was rendered defenceless as they deliberately attempted to kill her – what greater mental torture for a human being is there?”
The Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Kenya Records Ebola Case for First Time
articles.title_zh: Kenya Records Ebola Case for First Time
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has confirmed its first ever case of Ebola - a Kenyan citizen who has been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the past seven years.
Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient, who fell ill a month ago, and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo, died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
Duale said the patient boarded a flight on Saturday and underwent normal public screening at the main airport in Nairobi before he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city.
Kenya's health ministry says it has since stepped up surveillance at airports and border crossings.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
Since then, all known cases of the highly infectious disease have been in DR Congo.
The virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment.
​​There are however four vaccines in development, with human trials for one of them launched in July.
Duale confirmed that the Kenyan national had tested positive for the Bundibugyo species.
According to the minister, the patient first travelled by road from DR Congo to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi.
Duale said that after being taken to the Nairobi Hospital, the patient was transferred to an isolation facility that was built during the Covid-19 pandemic.
It was there that the patient "developed fever, chills, intense fatigue and weakness, painful swallowing, muscle pain and bleeding under the skin".
"Doctors suspected a viral haemorrhagic fever based on his symptoms and travel history and collected samples for testing. The sample tested positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus," Duale said.
The patient died at 23:30 (20:30 GMT) on Monday and he was buried on Tuesday in line with public health safety protocols.
At least 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, have been identified, while health authorities are tracing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight.
A senior health ministry official said the patient might have passed screening at the airport because the medication he was taking masked his symptoms.
Kenya introduced tighter checks at airports and border posts after the outbreak was declared in DR Congo but these have now been further intensified.
The health minister urged Kenyans "not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease".
He asked health workers to be "extra vigilant and maintain the highest infection prevention and control measures regardless of the condition being treated".
The WHO has recorded 4,114 deaths out of 8,544 cases in the current outbreak, making it the largest ever recorded in DR Congo, where Ebola was first discovered in 1976.
Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) believes the current toll could be even higher because of gaps in surveillance and testing in the war-torn country.
On Monday, MSF said the virus was spreading "like a megafire", with new hotspots emerging in North Kivu province, which borders Ituri where the virus began.
Since early September this had "intensified dramatically" with the province now accounting for nearly 40% of all newly confirmed cases nationwide, MSF said.
Eastern DR Congo has been riven by decades of conflict, with multiple rebel groups operating in the region amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources.
The crisis has led to the death and displacement of millions of people, and  hampered the country's ability to develop and maintain functional health care systems and infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: New York Is The Best City In The World, According To New Study
articles.title_zh: New York Is The Best City In The World, According To New Study
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
In no surprise at all to New Yorkers, New York City was just ranked as the world's best city.
Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index looked at the 1,000 largest cities across the globe, ranking each metropolis on various factors that indicate that location's strength, stability, and opportunity.
Economics, human capital, quality of life, environment, and governance were examined for each city, and received a score of up to 100. European and North American cities dominate 78 of the first 100 spots in the rankings. This index is designed to help businesses, governments and investors compare cities through streamlined data, which can help assess financial and business opportunities. The data does not look at human rights, which can be found in rankings like the Human Rights Foundation's Municipal Equality Index .
New to the annual index is an interactive feature for users to compare their cities based on these factors. With a population of about 485,000 people, Canberra, Australia, for example, is ranked at number 45 on the list but is the only city on the index that earned a perfect 100 for quality of life. Honolulu, Hawaii is the 124th city overall, but the only city with a perfect environmental score. Both Copenhagen and Aarhus, Denmark, which are about a 3 hour drive or train ride from each other, are the only two places with 100 for governance; though Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch, New Zealand all came in pretty close at 99.1.
New York City, which ranked first on the entire list, received a score of 100 for economics, 89.5 for human capital, 80.8 for quality of life, 72.8 for environment, and 75.7 for governance. This is the third consecutive year New York has held the top rating on the annual index. New York City is home to over 8.58 million people, with about 1 million people commuting in and out of the five boroughs every day. According to data from New York City Tourism, 65 million tourists visited New York City last year.
With a population of 9.1 million people, London, England came in second, with a score of 100 for human capital but just 86.5 for economics. Paris, France is in third, with no perfect score in any category, followed by two more U.S. cities: Seattle and San Francisco. Sixth place on the list goes to Dublin, Ireland, followed by Boston, San Jose, Tokyo, and then Zurich in 10th place.
Beyond the top list, Oxford Economics also ranked the top cities to watch. This section highlights five cities per region that may be underrepresented on the current list, but seem likely to climb in the rankings due to ongoing growth, opportunity, and potential.
Highest ranking on the cities to watch list include Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates and Riyadh in Saudi Arabia. In the U.S., San Antonio, Texas; Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; and Jacksonville, Florida are all named cities to watch.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

articles.title_orig: Tropical Depression 9 forms in Gulf. What does that mean for Texas?
articles.title_zh: Tropical Depression 9 forms in Gulf. What does that mean for Texas?
articles.content_orig:
HOUSTON - Texas has its eyes peeled on the southern Gulf where Tropical Depression 9 formed Tuesday.
The system, which had been designated Invest 92L, is located in the Bay of Campeche.
According to the forecast from the National Hurricane Center, Tropical Depression 9 will stay east of Texas. It is forecast to come ashore along the northern Gulf Coast later this week.
Tropical Depression 9 is forecast to become Tropical Storm Isaias by Tuesday night or Wednesday morning, and then become the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season by Thursday.
Most computer forecast models agree that Tropical Depression 9 will not be a big problem for Texas. However, anytime there is a tropical system in the Gulf, it is worth watching closely.
It doesn’t take a landfalling tropical system to cause problems for coastal Texas. With a system in the Gulf, rip currents and coastal flooding can become problems in addition to the heavy rain and gusty winds that they can bring.
The National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi has issued a coastal flood advisory for the barrier islands until 7 p.m. Tuesday. Forecasters said water could be pushed up to beach dunes on the Aransas, Kleberg, Nueces and Calhoun islands. This can lead to difficult driving and blocked roads.
Parts of the Texas coast will also see enhanced rainfall chances this weekend as the system moves toward the northern Gulf Coast, but the amounts look manageable at this time.
The Source: Information in this story came from the National Hurricane Center, the National Weather Service and FOX Weather.

articles.title_zh: Yemeni government fighters shown driving vehicles over Houthi opponents
articles.content_orig:
A U.S.-run military air base in England faced Iranian-related threats, and the Trump administration believes the intention was to kill as many American troops and destroy as many U.S. planes as possible, a U.S. official told The Associated Press.
The official, who was not authorized to comment publicly on the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity, could not speak to the nature of the potential attack. The United States removed its bombers from RAF Fairford , located 100 miles west of London, which has been used by American planes to strike Iran during this year's war.
President Trump told reporters on Monday he didn't want to tempt "the enemy" by having the bombers there.
The new details come as British police on Tuesday arrested a 22-year-old British man in central London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. He is the seventh person arrested in connection with the suspected plot against RAF Fairford, which authorities have linked to Iran. But British police so far have released few details of their investigation.
Six of the men arrested have since been released on bail, which drew criticism from Mr. Trump last week .
Iran summoned French ambassador to Tehran, Pierre Cochard, on Tuesday over Paris's treatment of protesters demanding better conditions in schools, state media reported, with French police having clashed for days with demonstrators.
Iran accused France of "violent treatment" of the protesters and "extensive and flagrant human rights violations" during the demonstrations, which began late last month and have been accompanied by unrest.
Relations between France and Iran have been strained for months, with the two expelling each other's diplomats in August.
Iran itself suffered major anti-government protests in January, during which the authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, blaming "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Foreign-based NGOs maintain that security forces fired on protesters.
Most families of the six soldiers killed in the deadliest attack of the Iran war will not be attending a major White House event for Gold Star families hosted by President Trump.
Only one family member of those killed in an Iranian drone strike March 1 on Port Shuaiba in Kuwait confirmed to The Associated Press that they planned to attend Tuesday's reception with Mr. Trump and the first lady.
"There are questions about what happened before the attack, what information was available, what decisions were made, and what happened in the moments leading up to six American soldiers losing their lives," Joey Amor — whose 39-year-old wife, Master Sgt. Nicole M. Amor , was among those killed — said in a public Facebook statement Monday. "I am done asking quietly. Today, I am asking the American people to stand with these six families and demand transparency."
Some Gold Star families say they are grateful for how the Trump administration and military have honored their loved one's sacrifice. Other families say the way the White House has handled the reception is the latest indication that the administration does not respect the price they have paid.
The spouse of Maj. Alex Klinner, an airman who was killed in an Iran-related combat operation this summer, said receiving less than two weeks' notice did not give her enough time to arrange for overnight care for her three young children.
In a text message, Libby Klinner said she would not have gone anyway, adding, "I have no interest in supporting an administration that has been so reckless with the lives of our service members."
The war, launched Feb. 28, has claimed the lives of 19 U.S. troops and wounded more than 800 others.
The Houthis were fighting Tuesday around Dhubab, a strategic town in Yemen that its internationally-recognized government had previously said it had retaken, a senior Yemeni military official told The Associated Press. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters.
Joined by its Yemeni government allies, Saudi Arabia is leading a coalition to attack Houthi military targets in Yemen. Their offensive follows the government's announcement on Sunday, declaring a campaign to reclaim Houthi-controlled territories in the country. Fighting has been concentrated in a region near the southern tip of the Red Sea to prevent disruptions to oil and gas exports.
The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said on Tuesday that its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at a city in Saudi Arabia's southwest.
The coalition's spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said on X that it "intercepted and destroyed" the missile launched towards Khamis Mushait, which is home to an air base.
U.S. military officials on Tuesday denied Iranian state media's reports of a downed U.S. Navy helicopter in the Red Sea.
"Iranian state media has been pushing false reports that a U.S. Navy MH-60R helicopter crashed in the Red Sea after declaring an emergency last night," U.S. Central Command wrote in a post on X .
CENTCOM said the reports were "not true" and that "all U.S. military aircraft and personnel across the Middle East are safe and unaccounted for."
Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, dismissed U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's latest statements on Iran, calling his forecasts "delusional" and accusing Washington of propaganda.
"Bessent's delusional forecasts never had any credibility in the first place. His latest propaganda will have an equally short shelf life," Rezaei wrote on X.
He added: "You lost the military war. You will fail in the economic war, too. Hormuz will not be opened by threats or pressure. Iran will not back down."
The White House on Tuesday denied that President Trump suggested Iran should "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego.
At a campaign rally in Nebraska, Mr. Trump called the Iran war "artificial," but added that he wanted to see a "total victory." He suggested the war was a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe."
"They can take out a city," Mr. Trump said, alluding to the risk of Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon. "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego."
Attendees cheered after his remark. It was not immediately clear what Mr. Trump meant, but the comments were quickly condemned by California Gov. Gavin Newsom and other state officials.
White House spokesperson Steven Cheung posted Tuesday on X that "the media freakout" over Mr. Trump's remarks was "not rooted in reality."
"He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung argued. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money."
Three Iranian men went on trial in the U.K. Tuesday on charges of spying for Iran, allegedly laying the groundwork for a violent attack against at least one London-based journalist.
The Iranian nationals visited addresses linked to people including two journalists working for the Farsi-language Iran International television network, which Tehran has long labeled a terror organization.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, who have all pleaded not guilty, appeared at a court in London accompanied by translators Tuesday.
Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones told the jury the three were accused of conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service, "in other words ... they spied on people of interest to the Iranian regime."
Another of the men's targets was lawyer Jonathan Turner, a founding member of the group U.K. Lawyers for Israel.
The three accused men do not deny visiting the addresses and taking photos and videos, but Sepahvand claimed he had been coerced and acted out of fear, the prosecution said.
Manesh and Noori said they were not aware that what they were doing was to assist the Iranian intelligence services, the prosecution added.

articles.title_orig: White House, DOJ pushed FBI to investigate protesters, violating rights: Whistleblower
articles.title_zh: White House, DOJ pushed FBI to investigate protesters, violating rights: Whistleblower
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration pushed the FBI to investigate Los Angeles protesters in violation of their constitutional rights and the bureau’s policies, a former FBI supervisor alleges in a new whistleblower complaint.
Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, made a formal whistleblower complaint to Senate Judiciary Committee leaders over the federal response to anti-ICE protest activity around federal buildings, as well as in a residential area, early last year.
Fields asked Congress and the Justice Department’s watchdog to investigate the allegations, her attorneys said in a letter to lawmakers. She says they violated the First Amendment right to free speech and to peaceably assemble.
Fields says Emil Bove, then the acting deputy attorney general, told the head of the field office to open an investigation into activities outside the federal building even though, she says, the activities were protected free speech. Separately, she says the White House gave a directive to FBI Director Kash Patel to investigate a group of protesters using megaphones during immigration enforcement operations after FBI agents had conducted a check into the conduct and declined to open an investigation.
President Donald Trump had viewed a video of people using megaphones to alert residents about immigration activities, advise them of their legal rights and encourage them not to open their doors unless immigration enforcement agents had signed judicial warrants, according to the letter.
A person whose name is redacted in the complaint told Fields that an investigation would be opened because “the President wants this investigation,” Fields’ whistleblower complaint says.
The protests were staged across Los Angeles after the Trump administration launched an immigration enforcement operation. Fields said the FBI’s Los Angeles office had pulled agents off active cartel cases to satisfy what a supervisor described as “optics” designed to “make a show for the president.” The area would be the scene of major protests later in the year during an immigration surge in cities nationwide.
A Justice Department spokesperson called the whistleblower complaint politically motivated and said violence is not protected by the First Amendment, though the complaint focused on nonviolent protests.
“Under President Trump, the Department of Justice will continue to vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law,” the spokesperson said. “The DOJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law.”
The FBI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Justice Department officials have previously said government workers need to follow the Trump administration’s priorities. Last week, Justice Department leaders filed an administrative complaint about federal judges who made remarks to the media about the impact the surge in immigration enforcement had on their courtrooms.
Fields says supervisors were told not to put things in writing, so many of the directives came in face-to-face meetings. She says she didn’t know whether any formal investigation was opened because she was excluded once she refused to participate.
Fields consulted with a senior FBI official in charge of privacy and civil liberties matters, who expressed dismay about the investigation and subsequently told Fields she planned to resign, according to the complaint.
Fields, too, resigned from the bureau, after she was informed that she would be removed from heading three programs, a decision she believes constituted retaliation for making protected internal disclosures. The FBI’s actions, according to the letter, “created a chilling effect within the workforce” and “signaled to other employees that raising constitutional or legal concerns could carry professional consequences.”
The conduct “had significant consequences for constitutional rights, and the integrity and effective operation of the FBI,” according to the complaint.
Hundreds of FBI agents and Justice Department attorneys have resigned or been fired since Trump returned to office , particularly those who were involved in investigating him, and former Justice Department employees have expressed concerns that the nation’s top law enforcement agency is doing the bidding of the president.
Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., told NBC News that Fields’ disclosure is another instance of Trump’s weaponizing the Justice Department to go after his perceived political enemies. Padilla, who himself was forcibly removed from a news conference featuring then-Homeland Security Kristi Noem in June 2025 , is the ranking member of the Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, citizenship and border safety.
“How many more of these investigations have been opened up because of political pressure coming from the White House, despite the questions and concerns about legality and constitutionality?” Padilla said.
He acknowledged that the Trump administration’s attacks on civil service protections through unilateral firings, as well as the mass firings of internal government watchdogs , had an impact on the legislative branch’s ability to conduct oversight.
“That’s going to be a significant challenge, but it begins with good, honorable professionals being willing to come forward and tell us what’s going on and what’s wrong with what’s going on,” Padilla said. “We’re hoping others may be inspired, as well.”
In a letter he sent to Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche, Padilla wrote that the allegations in the Fields disclosure “raise grave concerns about the rule of law under your leadership, the diversion of resources from ongoing criminal investigations, and the testimony that you provided under oath to Congress.”
He asked for officials to preserve information about the investigation and send any details to his office.
Fields was represented by the nonprofit Government Accountability Project and David Laufman, a former top official in the Justice Department’s National Security Section.
Ryan J. Reilly is a justice reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: $100B Trade Gap: China vs. US Data Exposed
articles.title_zh: $100B Trade Gap: China vs. US Data Exposed
articles.content_orig:
A staggering $100 billion discrepancy exists between China’s reported exports and the US’s recorded imports. Michael Kanko, CEO of ImportGenius.com, explains what this trade data delta signifies for the global supply chain. He details how granular shipping records are used for everything from sourcing new components to ensuring compliance with international sanctions, and why transparency in air cargo data is the next big battle for US manufacturers.
ImportGenius has identified a more than $100 billion gap between what China reported shipping to the United States last year and what U.S. records show as received — a discrepancy that highlights the limitations of relying on government trade statistics alone and the growing role of bill-of-lading data in supply chain intelligence.
The finding emerged when ImportGenius normalized its shipment-level data into TEUs — the standard 20-foot equivalent unit used in global container trade — and cross-referenced that count against U.S. Census dollar values to derive a value-per-container figure. Comparing that metric to China’s own TEU-normalized figures produced what the company described as a major and “mystifying” difference. Possible explanations include transshipment through third countries such as Vietnam, incorrectly recorded shipment values, and potential incentives tied to tariff optimization.
Beyond the macro discrepancy, Kanko said the platform’s users are increasingly tapping shipment records — which capture details down to the markings on individual boxes, container contents, shipper and consignee identities, and notified parties — for sourcing and compliance purposes. With sanctions at historically high levels due to ongoing conflicts, companies are using trade data to vet new customers. Kanko offered a concrete example: confirming whether an aviation parts buyer in Turkey had transacted with Russia within the past 30 days. Law enforcement and brand-protection teams, including major footwear manufacturers tracking counterfeit sneakers from Asia, are also users.
On near-term freight volumes, Kanko said he expects international ocean shipping activity to continue, and possibly intensify, through at least the midterm elections, citing persistent policy uncertainty as the primary driver. He also noted rising shipment activity out of Vietnam, Mexico, and other Asian and South American origins. ImportGenius recently gained access to Mexican shipment-level trade data, which also provides visibility into transborder land crossings between Mexico and the United States.
An emerging use case is domestic lead generation: U.S. manufacturers are now using the platform to identify importers of products similar to what they produce — essentially building prospect lists at a moment when the pricing dynamic has shifted in their favor relative to Chinese competitors. Kanko said this trend is notably stronger than when the company was founded nearly 20 years ago.
The company is also pushing for legislative change on air cargo transparency. Nearly half of U.S. imports by value arrive by air, yet no public manifest data exists for those shipments — a gap Kanko attributed to a law rooted in maritime trade that has not kept pace with air cargo’s growth since the 1970s. ImportGenius has spent three years advocating for the Manifest Modernization Act, which has companion bills in both the House and Senate and support from the Ways and Means Committee, the Senate Finance Committee, and the House China Select Committee. Kanko testified before the Ways and Means Committee and said the bill has drawn bipartisan co-sponsors. The company is also exploring whether the legislation could be attached to the annual defense reauthorization bill before year’s end.

articles.title_orig: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.title_zh: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.
California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as  "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.
Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.
Trump, while speaking on Monday in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."
There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.
The morning after Trump's statement, Governor Newsom announced that the "dangerous - if not treasonous" statement had prompted him to direct California's State Threat Assessment Center to "monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the remarks as an invitation" to target California.
The agency is designed to detect and prevent security threats in the state.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".
Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.
In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".
"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".
The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.
A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.
"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added.
San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.
It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.
Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.
It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.
This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.
Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent.
Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests.
Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities.

articles.title_orig: Ravens’ Marlon Humphrey, Tyler Loop to join Trump at Sparrows Point
articles.title_zh: Ravens’ Marlon Humphrey, Tyler Loop to join Trump at Sparrows Point
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump visited Maryland on Tuesday to announce a project that's expected to support 14,000 jobs and become the state's largest job creator in over a decade.
The president toured Tradepoint Atlantic with Anduril Industries, a defense technology firm in Sparrows Point, and announced that the former Bethlehem Steel site will be turned into a 2-million-square-foot shipyard to build components for Virginia-class attack submarines.
According to a media briefing, the components include torpedo tubes, sterns and bow sections, and will be built at the Sparrows Point site.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said this will be the largest private investment in the state in more than a decade.
"With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs," said Moore. "We thank Anduril for choosing Maryland, and we're ready to build the future of the aerospace and defense economy together."
The facility is expected to support 14,000 jobs, including the creation of 3,100 permanent jobs. Over a decade, Arsenal-2, the name of the new industrial base, will become the state's largest job creator.
"For generations, this site shaped America's steel and shipbuilding legacy, including its critical role during World War II, when workers here built the vessels that helped defend our nation," Baltimore County Executive Kathy Klausmeier said in a statement.
The $3.7 billion private capital investment will become the largest single private investment in the state.
Happening right now, @realDonaldTrump has taken the stage in Sparrows Point to officially announce @anduriltech ’s new shipyard to help create the next generation of submarines for the @USNavy ! @wbaltv11 pic.twitter.com/EhDT4ohBt2
"With Arsenal-2, Anduril will return large-scale shipbuilding to a site that can once again define American naval power. This facility will make Baltimore County a critical part of America's submarine industrial base, adding the production capacity that the Navy needs to meet its Virginia-class requirements," said Brian Schimpf, Anduril cofounder and CEO.
Under the agreement, the state and Baltimore County will match up to 13% of the anticipated investment through existing economic incentive programs and new appropriations.
The state would also support the construction of a workforce training facility near Tradepoint Atlantic.

articles.title_orig: McDonald's sued over AI tool that recommends prices to US franchisees
articles.title_zh: McDonald's sued over AI tool that recommends prices to US franchisees
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
McDonald's is facing a federal lawsuit that alleges its AI -enhanced pricing tool violates antitrust laws because it shares nonpublic data with franchisees who might be competing in the same market.
The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in Illinois, said McDonald's pricing tool uses artificial intelligence to collect data that competing franchises wouldn't normally share, like store-level sales. The Chicago-based burger giant has said it makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants.
The lawsuit also blames the pricing system for raising McDonald's U.S. prices.
"McDonald's has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of U.S. restaurants," the lawsuit states. "The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin."
McDonald's said Tuesday that the lawsuit is "filled with inaccuracies" and it would vigorously defend itself.
"AI does not set menu prices at McDonald's restaurants – McDonald's franchisees do," the company said in a statement. "Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way."
The lawsuit was filed on behalf of a consumer, Michael Thomas, of DeKalb, Illinois. According to the lawsuit, Thomas frequently visits McDonald's and orders a Quarter Pounder with cheese, french fries and a Coke. The lawsuit said Thomas noticed price differences between McDonald's stores near his home.
McDonald's said it has used an AI-enhanced pricing tool for more than a decade. The program determines the optimal price for menu items based on a store's sales, location and other factors, including competitors' prices.
McDonald's said that long before adopting the AI-enhanced tool, it collected data and recommended prices to its franchisees, who own and operate 95% of McDonald's 14,000 U.S. stores.
"All we do is provide the context of what's going on," a McDonald's spokesman told The Associated Press. "We don't have any way to affect the menu pricing in a restaurant."
But the lawsuit said McDonald's has "significant leverage over its franchisees" and can pressure them to follow its pricing recommendations.
The Associated Press left a message Tuesday with the National Owners Association, which represents McDonald's franchisees.
McDonald's has been experimenting with various value strategies in the U.S. and other markets for several years as it tries to win back lower-income consumers, whose visits to fast-food chains have dropped.
But franchisees don't always follow its guidance. During a conference call with investors in August, McDonald's Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski said only 60% of its U.S. restaurants were offering McDonald's proposed menu of 10 items for under $3.
"As you know, in our system, that's not something that we just flip the switch on," Kempczinski said. "It requires conversations with franchisees."
The lawsuit asks the judge to certify the case as a class action and to require McDonald's to pay damages to the class. It also seeks to prevent McDonald's from enforcing agreements that restrict competition.

articles.title_orig: China Refiners Flock to Iraqi Crude
articles.title_zh: China Refiners Flock to Iraqi Crude
articles.content_orig:
China’s independent refiners are turning to Iraqi crude after a US blockade choked supplies from top source Iran, while competition from state-owned rivals priced most of them out of Russian barrels.
Private processors, including smaller ‘teapot’ refiners in Shandong province, have bought Iraq’s Basrah Heavy and Basrah Medium grades for November delivery at premiums of as much as $18 a barrel to ICE Brent, according to traders familiar with the matter. The purchases point to a rush for prompt supplies rather than a strong recovery in Chinese oil demand .
At least 50 tankers, mostly carrying Iranian crude, are bottled up along the nation’s coast as a US blockade seeks to pressure Tehran into ending the seven-month war on terms favorable to Washington. At the same time, state-owned Chinese refiners are taking most of the available Russian crude, driving up costs for independent processors.
Inventories at some Shandong teapots could run out as early as the end of this month, forcing refiners to compete for a shrinking pool of alternatives just as Beijing issued fresh crude-import quotas, said Muyu Xu, senior crude analyst at Kpler. “To avoid shutting down or significantly cutting run rates, refiners need to secure alternative supplies as soon as possible.”
The supply squeeze has pushed some processors toward sulfur-rich Basrah crude, which they typically avoid in favor of cheaper Iranian barrels and diesel-rich ESPO from Russia’s Far East.
Improving Middle Eastern flows , as Gulf producers move more oil through the Strait of Hormuz, are also making Iraqi crude increasingly accessible. Producers in the region are deepening discounts to defend market share after Saudi Aramco cut the price of its flagship grade for Asian buyers.
Meanwhile, Russian barrels remain expensive, with ESPO commanding a premium of almost $30 a barrel above Brent, the traders said, asking not to be identified as the negotiations are private.
“Teapots are very price sensitive,” Kpler’s Muyu Xu said, adding that Basrah is now cheaper than Russia’s ESPO, making those barrels increasingly attractive to private refiners.
Buyers of Iraqi crude include both private processors in China’s Shandong province and some large independent refiners, according to the traders. Iraqi barrels are typically marketed by trading houses such as Vitol Group, Trafigura Group and Mercuria Energy Group, as well as TotalEnergies SE.
Iran was a major crude supplier to China’s independent refiners before the blockade, with imports exceeding 1 million barrels a day prior to the war. Private processors were the main buyers, attracted by steep discounts on sanctioned barrels that bolstered refining margins.
