articles.title_orig: Liberal justices look for 'escape hatch' as high-stakes climate case lands at Supreme Court, experts say
articles.title_zh: Liberal justices look for 'escape hatch' as high-stakes climate case lands at Supreme Court, experts say
articles.content_orig:
Utah and Alabama attorneys general warn Colorado’s climate case could drive up costs nationwide, while former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee argues Americans harmed by climate change deserve their day in court.
Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor's repeated questions concerning whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear a high-profile climate case that could expose oil companies to lawsuits across the country steered conservative lawyers to believe that the liberal justices are seeking an "off-ramp."
"The fact that they kept going back to trying to create a jurisdictional problem tells me they don't feel confident that they have the votes in this space," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, a conservative judicial group, told Fox News Digital. "Jackson and Sotomayor were looking for an escape hatch."
The Supreme Court began its new term Monday, hearing its first oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder, in which they will rule on whether state tort laws can be used to seek damages from oil companies for climate change, even when the alleged harms are occurring outside the state or continent. The justices will also rule on whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear this case now, as the case is still before the Colorado Supreme Court .
The case before the high court is in an unusual procedural posture, meaning the justices could resolve it without ever reaching the blockbuster state-versus-federal power fight at its center. That dispute centers on whether Colorado can use its own laws to seek damages for alleged harms caused by emissions from other states or whether it's an issue for the federal government and Congress to regulate.
Climate activist protesters gather outside the Supreme Court before oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder on Oct. 5, 2025. (Elaine Mallon/Fox News Digital)
SUPREME COURT BEGINS NEW TERM WITH HIGH-PROFILE LOOK AT CLEAN AIR AND FEDERAL AUTHORITY
"The questions by Jackson and Sotomayor trying to say it would be premature for the court to issue an opinion are simply the liberal justices trying to find an off-ramp for the case because they are afraid they will be outvoted on the main issue: does federal law such as the Clean Air Act preempt all state claims like those asserted here," Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow with Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital.
While questioning Suncor attorney Kannon Shanmugam, Jackson suggested the dispute may have reached the Supreme Court too soon, calling it "premature from the standpoint of this court exercising its jurisdiction."
She also repeatedly questioned why the court couldn't wait to hear the case, saying the court doesn't "have the whole set of facts" and that the court doesn't "really know enough to be confident" that the theories posed are applicable.
"It feels to me like the defendants ... are bringing it back to federal court before the state courts have really had a chance to sort out who is the source, what is their allegation with respect to how this causation is happening," Jackson told Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who argued in support of Suncor.
Meanwhile, Sotomayor refused to drop her line of questioning on jurisdiction with Shanmugam, proposing that the Supreme Court send the case back to the Colorado Supreme Court.
"If we're unsure of your characterization, because there's certainly a number of amici brief who disagree with that characterization, shouldn't we be certifying this question to the Colorado court instead of us deciding it? We have to be sure of our jurisdiction before we take it," Sotomayor said.
Republican Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall told Fox News Digital it was clear that the liberal justices were trying to cast doubt on whether they have jurisdiction.
Climate activists gather outside the Supreme Court for oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder on Oct. 5, 2026. (Elaine Mallon/Fox News Digital)
SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA
"Well, I think you saw both Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor try to find an out for this court, basically saying the court doesn't have jurisdiction at this stage of the case to be able to make a final ruling. I think that you saw the advocates on behalf of Suncor be able to distinguish that."
If the Supreme Court declines to reach the federalism issue, the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling allowing Boulder's state-law claims to proceed would remain in place, leaving the broader question of how far states can use tort law to pursue climate claims against energy companies unresolved.
Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Boulder attorney Kevin Russell on whether a Boulder win could trigger similar lawsuits nationwide. Russell said there are legal limits, but acknowledged to Justice Clarence Thomas that Boulder's theory could allow other fossil-fuel businesses to be sued.
"The chief justice and the court do not like issuing rulings with no limiting principles, rulings that could open up unlimited litigation and claims. Kannon Shanmugam, the lawyer for Suncor, emphasized this again at the very end of the oral argument when he pointed out that there are not only 90,000 political jurisdictions that could sue, but individuals could also sue claiming damages from global warming," von Spakovsky said.
"And he also pointed out something the conservative majority frowns upon: that Boulder is trying to resolve a major policy issue in the courts instead of in the legislative branches," von Spakovsky continued.
Conservative lawyers believe that Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor are seeking an "off-ramp." (Getty Images)
SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE
Supporters of Suncor say the lawsuits could "bankrupt" oil companies and cause the price for consumers to go up.
"It's to basically create a carbon tax on both producers and emitters across the country, which would include, by the way, my cattlemen in Alabama producing beef for our country, those that are creating concrete to be able to build structures and be able to grow our economy," Marshall told Fox News. "They ultimately want to bankrupt that industry to have their preferred climate change policies be in play."
"They're literally addressing behavior that takes place all over the world," Utah Attorney General Derek Brown told Fox News Digital. "They want to regulate not just what happens in Colorado, but what happens in my state of Utah or in Saudi Arabia. That's not the way the system works. So, really, this case comes down to one main issue and that is who gets to decide things like energy policy. And ultimately, under our system, it should be Congress."
Meanwhile, Boulder alleged ExxonMobil and Suncor knew for decades about the climate risks associated with fossil fuels but misled the public about those risks. The communities estimate that taxpayers could face more than $100 million in costs to adapt to climate-related impacts, including wildfires, drought and damage to roads and other infrastructure.
Former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat and longtime advocate for aggressive action on climate change, argued those costs are already being felt by communities across the country.
"As governor, I've worked with so many families who've lost their homes," Inslee told Fox News Digital. "So many communities have essentially burned down, and they ought to be able to have a day in court to hear the evidence, to determine whether the lies of the oil and gas industry legitimately, they make it so that they're held accountable."
The complaint pointed to a 1977 internal memo from ExxonMobil that circulated among the company's highest-level managers. The memo reported that "current scientific opinion overwhelmingly favors" that fossil fuels contribute to the rise in CO2 emissions.

articles.title_orig: ‘Carrie’ expands its story for the modern world with an exceptional, apocalyptic lead
articles.title_zh: ‘Carrie’ expands its story for the modern world with an exceptional, apocalyptic lead
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Published in 1974, Stephen King’s first novel, “Carrie,” sold a million copies in its first year, and millions more after the appearance of Brian De Palma’s 1976 film adaptation, which, if we are to trust Wikipedia, made nearly $139 million on a budget of $1.8 million. (That’s not even counting what home video has teleported into corporate pockets in the years since, laying the foundation of the King Industrial Entertainment Complex.)
A springboard in the careers of De Palma, Sissy Spacek, John Travolta, Nancy Allen and Amy Irving, De Palma’s “Carrie” is an excellent film that, having seen it once, I never want to see again, the bullying and humiliation of a perfectly nice if slightly strange young woman being my idea of no fun, even if it does lead to a spectacular set piece.
And so the prospect of watching an eight-hour adaptation of the novel stretched out before me like a five-year semester in which every class was P.E. But here we are, with “Carrie” 2026, developed (and directed in part) by Mike Flanagan ( “The Haunting of Hill House” ), premiering Wednesday on Prime Video.
When Mike Flanagan decided to revamp Stephen King’s horror classic, he brought Carrie and her mother, Margaret, to the present as they contend with the outside world’s cruelty.
Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) lives with her mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) and father Ralph (Tahmoh Penikett), a conspiracy-minded construction worker, in a sort of cult of three, out of which Carrie has never been allowed to poke her head. (For some reason, we are in “Chamberlain, USA,” and not the canonical Maine; it was filmed in Vancouver, of course.) Though “a loner” and “a bit of a doomsday prepper,” Dad is seemingly not a bad guy — Carrie loves him, anyway — but he departs the series early in a manner that will raise the eyebrows of anyone familiar with the paranormal phenomena at the heart of the story, and so many stories to come. His death prompts a visit from social services, and Carrie is sent to high school, where she begins as a sophomore, though every student she’ll interact with is a senior, while mom is sentenced to work, in a low-level service job in a world she was never made for and that frankly disgusts her.
Carrie, whose natural, long-bottled curiosity has been fed by the books a kind neighbor, Stella (Naika Toussaint), has secretly slipped her over the years, is excited to go to school, where they have computers and a library and other people, but her newness, oddness and 19th century home-sewn clothes make her a target. Things go bad when she gets her first period in the girls’ locker room and having been told nothing by her mother about menstruation believes she is dying. The crowd’s reaction to this is to pelt her with tampons. Teenagers!
The ringleader in this is Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton), chief mean girl, whose nicer best friend is Sue Snell (Siena Agudong); we’ll meet Sue near the top of the series telling an unseen interlocutor, “It’s so easy to forget ... we were kids.” In accordance with Flanagan’s scheme to build dimension into King’s characters, Chris is not merely a mean girl — she is a sad mean girl, about to learn that she is no longer rich, flattening her dream of going to Duke with Sue, and that her mother (Heather Graham) may not be coming home, which, as we’ve met her very unpleasant father (Michael Trucco), seems the sane move. She’ll compensate by hooking up with Billy Nolan (Arthur Conti), a high school dropout — or someone who was kicked out (described as “the reason we have metal detectors” at Ewen High) — minor league drug dealer and pig farmer (she will find this last occupation handy, come the story’s signature prank).
There are the now-traditional scenes in which Carrie learns to consciously control her telekinetic superpowers, previously manifested by accidentally setting off car alarms, opening mailboxes and causing a rain of rocks on her parents’ roof. Arms out, fingers splayed, she takes a comic-book summoning pose familiar from decades of mutant movies. (The business of superpowers arriving with the onset of puberty will become a dog-eared trope of science fiction.) There’s a lot of Carrie in Eleven, from “Stranger Things,” and a little of “Stranger Things” in this “Carrie.”
“We’re allowed to read all of them?” asks Carrie, when shown the school library. (We will see her with a stack of books, including “I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings,” “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest” and Malinda Lo’s “Last Night at the Telegraph Club,” described by Kirkus Review as “the intersectional, lesbian, historical teen novel so many readers have been waiting for.”) In my version of “Carrie,” she just hangs out there the whole time and avoids the haters. Maybe joins a book club and meets some fellow bibliophiles. Most often, when she seems on the verge of acceptance, happiness is snatched back from her — a nasty game. She does seem to make a friend with the appearance of Emaline West (Thalia Dudek), a Flanagan invention, a kind of devilish, yet supportive Jiminy Cricket figure who recognizes Carrie’s special powers.
“Through most of history I’d get drowned in a river, tortured on the rack or burned at the stake,” says Carrie, who has been reading about her condition, to Emaline, echoing the “documentary” sections that introduce each episode, offering background on the history of women with special powers in a male-dominated world (Joan of Arc, et al.), not that the story at hand really goes down that road. But it’s a point.
Other not insignificant characters I haven’t found a place to mention include Sue’s boyfriend, Tommy Ross (Joel Oulette), a sensitive jock; Josie Totah as Tina Blake, a secondary mean girl; Matthew Lillard, who will always be Shaggy to me, as beleaguered principal Henry Grayle; Amber Midthunder as Rita Desjardin, a sympathetic teacher; and Tim Bagley as Peter Morton, a sympathetic guidance counselor, who trades favorite literary quotes with Carrie. “Oh, um, I don’t do scary,” she says when he offers a line from “Frankenstein, “Nothing is so painful to the human mind as a great and sudden change.”
The eight-hour length has its good and bad points. King provided just enough material for a speedy feature, and so the series has been packed with extras. There are some useless side plots and some frankly wacky major interpolations in the later episodes, some of which appear to be laying the groundwork for a very different second season; Flanagan has in fact bruited a three-season arc, reaching far past the novel. The 20th century text is updated with notes on cyberbullying, viral videos , school shootings, conspiracy thinking, conservative populism, book banning and even beer pong. (Carrie goes to a party.) It can come across as polemical and yet somehow unavoidable.
But the more productive expansion has to do with character, especially as regards Carrie and her mother, who is not the deranged, abusive religious fanatic of previous versions, but an essentially loving parent frightened of the modern world. (She gets a surprising original arc in the back half of the series.) Whatever plot, or sinkholes may open in the larger narrative — I had more than a few “yes, but” reactions to elements of the story — “Carrie” does extremely well with person-to-person scenes. For all the cinematic energy and finesse dedicated to its climactic apocalypse (not a spoiler, it’s previewed at the start, and you may know it anyway), the real strength of the series is in quiet, one-on-one conversation, expressing issues of adolescent angst, loneliness and identity and generational and cultural divides that could serve any ordinary, non-paranormal teenage drama. Howell and Sloyan are quite wonderful in these moments, and Howell is exceptional throughout.
For all its little hiccups, “Carrie” does make one feel sad

articles.title_orig: Whistleblower suit alleges Trump ordered FBI investigation on LA anti-ICE protesters
articles.title_zh: Whistleblower suit alleges Trump ordered FBI investigation on LA anti-ICE protesters
articles.content_orig:
White House denies the allegations as ‘false’ and says ‘first amendment does not protect violent rioting’
US politics live – latest updates
Donald Trump ordered the FBI to investigate protesters in Los Angeles who were demonstrating against the president’s immigration crackdown, according to a whistleblower complaint.
Alex Padilla, a Democratic senator who represents California and serves on the Senate judiciary committee, said his office had received a copy of the complaint, which makes sweeping allegations about the Trump administration’s response to protests in LA in early 2025.
Demonstrators had been protesting against Trump’s deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to push the president’s agenda.
“These allegations are deeply alarming,” Padilla, who also serves as the top Democrat on the border security and immigration subcommittee, said in a statement. “Using the FBI to target Americans for exercising their first amendment rights directly undermines our nation’s foundational values. I won’t rest until we get answers.”
NBC first reported on the allegations after viewing a copy of the disclosure, which identifies the whistleblower as Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office, who made the complaint following the federal response to anti-ICE protests around the city’s federal buildings, and in residential area, in February last year.
Fields alleges that Emil Bove, then the acting deputy attorney general, told Akil Davis, the head of the field office, to open an investigation into protesters’ activities outside federal buildings, even though Fields says the demonstrations were protected free speech, and several FBI employees expressed concern with the legality of these requests.
Field, who joined the FBI in May 2016, also alleges that Trump reportedly viewed a TikTok video of protesters in Alhambra, California, that alerted neighbors about the presence of federal immigration officers and advised them of their legal rights. The White House, Fields says, then instructed Patel to direct the Los Angeles field office to initiate an investigation into those demonstrating in the video, because the president “was angry about the incident”.
Despite the fact that member of Fields’s team determined that the protesters’ actions were constitutionally protected and there was insufficient evidence, Fields was told by a colleague – whose name is redacted – that “the president wants this investigation”. Fields says that even though her supervisor acknowledged the investigation was unconstitutional, the directive still had to be followed.
Fields alleges that a “dedicated immigration squad” was created, comprising 10 agents, some of whom were taken off active cartel cases to carry out the White House’s requests. Fields says that she questioned the directives “operational logic” but her supervisor – whose name is also redacted in the complaint – described the move as “optics” designed to “make a show for the president”.
Fields says, however, she was not aware of any “actual or potential national security threat, federal criminal activity, or vulnerability” that would have warranted conducting assessments or opening investigations into anti-ICE and CBP protesters at the time.
She ultimately resigned from the bureau last year after she was removed from overseeing several programs, and believes that her diminished role was the result of objecting to protest-related investigations, according to the complaint.
after newsletter promotion
A White House spokesperson, Lauren Bis, called the allegations “false” in a statement to the Guardian. “The first amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” she said. “Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime. This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
Meanwhile, the FBI and justice department said in a joint statement they would “continue to vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law”.
“The DoJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law. Violence is not protected by the First Amendment. Politically motivated attacks will not deter us from doing our job,” they added.
In a letter to attorney general Todd Blanche and Patel, Padilla outlined Fields’s allegations and asked the officials dozens of questions about the reported investigations – including whether they resulted in arrests, how many directives of this kind the justice department has received from the president and the number of investigations that are still open.

articles.title_orig: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
articles.title_zh: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
articles.content_orig:
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes, western France, Tuesday. Jeremias Gonzalez/AP hide caption
PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron's nearly decade-long tenure.
"We need to listen to them," said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. "They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It's important to show that there are adults who support them."
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.
Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes, western France, Tuesday. Jeremias Gonzalez/AP hide caption
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in "almost all cases" and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students' concerns and find solutions.
Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced "ultra violence" threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any "accidents" would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a "lie."
More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make "any sense to hit minors."
"Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas," said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
Students chant slogans during a demonstration against under-resourced schools, in Paris, Tuesday. Teresa Suarez/AP hide caption
The violence is "absolutely unbearable," Le Coq said.
Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term.
Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
"You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.
Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.
At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.
"They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children's rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands," said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.
Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."
Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.
"So, we really need to act now, and it's in the government's hands, to see these demands through to the end," she said. "It's a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country."
Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday and several police injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.

articles.title_orig: They told the world AI was dangerous. Now Trump’s allies are coming for them.
articles.title_zh: They told the world AI was dangerous. Now Trump’s allies are coming for them.
articles.content_orig:
BERKELEY, Calif. - After artificial intelligence safety advocates captured Washington's attention with dire warnings about the technology's power, the Trump administration and its allies embraced some of their suggestions, while moving to sideline the advocates themselves.
Battle lines have been drawn in recent days over part of an accord signed by President Donald Trump and AI chief executives last week: Who should audit AI companies' systems to ensure their technology behaves as intended.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.
Leading AI companies - including OpenAI and Anthropic - have for years worked with a cluster of nonprofits concentrated in the Bay Area's AI safety community, which grew out of the effective altruism movement. But Trump's tech-world allies say the work of auditing AI should be taken on by America's largest consulting firms.
"In my view they should be professional auditors, not these NGOs," investor and former top White House AI adviser David Sacks said on his All-In podcast last week. He said in a post on X last month that the AI safety nonprofit METR, which has worked with Anthropic, was too close to the company to be called independent. Soon after, Anthropic said it would partner with consulting giant Accenture to build a team of outside evaluators.
At a conference here over the weekend, members of AI safety organizations grappled with the impact of what some see as a coordinated campaign to delegitimize their work and paint their community as cultish and unserious. The event took place at a former hotel popular with AI safety acolytes that also recently hosted a conference on AI consciousness and a sex workshop called "Slutcon."
Trump officials and allies have sniped at the movement for months but the attacks intensified after public anxiety over AI risks forced the White House to respond. Sacks last month shared on X a New York Post front page that called employees of METR, which helped OpenAI investigate its rogue AI agents, "THE WOKE WIZARDS OF AI." (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)
Trump on Sunday named several figures who have rejected calls from advocates for an AI industry-wide slowdown to his Super Intelligence Force advisory panel. They include Sacks and Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer, who said last month that calls for action to prevent extreme scenarios of AI causing harm promoted "extinction, death-cult-like philosophies."
"There has absolutely been a rhetorical push within certain corners of the White House and broader Trump administration to get the message out about effective altruism and its potential dangers," said a Trump administration official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe private discussions.
A White House official said that it supports organizations that evaluate the security and safety of how AI models are engineered. The official pointed to Trump's 2025 executive order targeting what the president termed "woke AI."
Anthropic declined to comment.
Nathan Leamer, director of the pro-industry nonprofit Build American AI, said he has been briefing congressional staff and other influential conservative figures in Washington about effective altruism, describing it as antithetical to his own Christian values.
"A year ago no one in Hill offices knew what effective altruism was," Leamer said. Build American AI is linked to Leading the Future, a political campaign group funded by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, a major midterms Republican donor.
Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, which says it is focused on AI policy in the public interest, said that Trump allies are trying discredit anyone pushing for meaningful AI regulation, an idea that now has significant momentum.
"In D.C., at least, and maybe in the broader culture, we won that fight. The vibe is with us," said Carson, who also leads a political advocacy organization funded in part by Anthropic. "People are very concerned. Congress wants to regulate."
But leaders of AI evaluation start-ups that did not grow out of the AI safety movement said some Washington Republicans are distrustful of the label.
"It almost felt like a new version of McCarthyism," said Rayan Krishnan, CEO of the Andreessen Horowitz-backed start-up Vals AI, after a trip to Washington last month to pitch his start-up to the public sector.
Judd Rosenblatt, CEO of AE Studio, who described himself as a conservative small business owner, said multiple people in the Trump administration have told his team that they see the need for third parties to assess AI tools, but are wary of effective altruism, he said.
Civil society groups that have been auditing AI systems since before the debut of ChatGPT warn there is a risk that an opportunity for oversight of opaque AI giants will be squandered.
"Where we find ourselves now is trying to determine who will actually be in the room in making decisions," said Miranda Bogen, chief technologist at the Center for Democracy & Technology and director of the advocacy group's AI Governance Lab, one of various groups eager to contribute their expertise in standard-setting.
The accord signed by AI chief executives last week, which Trump called "morally binding," was frequently mentioned onstage and in huddles between sessions at the Berkeley conference last weekend, where attendees endured a heat wave with fans and Popsicles.
At a Sunday discussion panel on what the AI auditor ecosystem might look like, one speaker said they are working on building a broad coalition of experts, including people working on bias and discrimination as well as blue-chip firms like Accenture and Deloitte. Panelists also discussed other ways the community could prove its legitimacy. Another suggested two-month boot camps to train a talent pipeline of qualified auditors.
Adam Gleave, CEO of FAR.AI, a nonprofit research institute, said in an interview that excluding the AI safety community would shut out people with expertise that are important in the current moment.
"When it comes to looking at millions of agent transcripts and trying to piece together what they did and how they were interacting, I don't think there are many organizations in the world that have that expertise," Gleave said. "The reality is that anyone you hire with that background is going to have some connection to the industry."
On his podcast, Sacks and his co-hosts, who remain close to the White House, made clear that they preferred instead to have established corporate giants do the work.
"You're going to see EY in short order here announce something," said investor Chamath Palihapitiya, who earlier in the episode said his start-up 8090 was building the global accounting firm formerly known as Ernst & Young "an entire audit infrastructure for super intelligence," and that 8090 now plans to "roll it out to everybody."
EY said in a statement that it was working with 8090 to "develop new capabilities that bring greater visibility, traceability and human accountability to consequential AI-enabled decisions and workflows."

articles.title_orig: “All things in the world must end”: Castro’s Mama Ji’s is closing at the end of the month
articles.title_zh: “All things in the world must end”: Castro’s Mama Ji’s is closing at the end of the month
articles.content_orig:
Rising rent puts an end to the dim sum and Sichuan restaurant that has been in the neighborhood for almost 15 years.
Mama Ji’s (opens in new tab) in the Castro was filled with diners Monday night. Waiters bustled around, moving between the compact dining room and sidewalk tables, shuttling plates of kung pao shrimp, triple “C” wings, and hot-and-numbing fish. They told diners about the night’s special, inspired by the most recent trip Lily Ji — customers know her as Mama Ji — took to the Sichuan province of China: crispy lotus-root cake topped with minced pork in fish sauce.
Judging by how busy the restaurant was, you’d never guess it would likely be diners’ final visits. The last day of service for Mama Ji’s, which opened almost 15 years ago, is set for Oct. 31.
Ji and her husband, Marv Wolpa, posted a letter on the door sharing the news and expressing gratitude for the neighbors who have supported their mom-and-pop restaurant but saying it is time for them to put their time and energy into their personal lives. “Work is a lot; I won’t miss the work,” Ji said. “But I will miss the people.”
In an interview with The Standard, Ji gave more context to the closure: The landlord had raised the rent, citing rising insurance costs and an inability to charge more for the residential unit above Mama Ji’s. “I said, ‘Whatever that’s your decision,’” Ji said. “That’s my decision to not continue.”
The couple, who are Castro residents, started serving the food Ji grew up eating as a pop-up, then transitioned to the full restaurant in 2013. Over the decade and a half the couple served their neighborhood, Mama Ji’s became a staple of the neighborhood.
One couple dining Monday night expressed their sadness. The waiter repeated what the letter said, noting that Ji and Wolpa are ready to retire. “All things in the world must end,” he concluded as he walked away.
As for Ji, she didn’t miss a beat when asked about what she plans to do next: “Relax!”
Madeline Taub is a food reporter intern at The Standard. She was previously a contributor to Cityside’s food publication, East Bay Nosh. She graduated from UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism.

articles.title_orig: School protests sweeping France cause 'heaviest toll in decades'
articles.title_zh: School protests sweeping France cause 'heaviest toll in decades'
articles.content_orig:
France is struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades. What started as a demonstration in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school to the north of Paris has snowballed into a national crisis.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close and more than 6,000 people have been taken into police custody over the past few weeks, most of them minors with no previous criminal records. Students, teachers and policemen have been injured. One student in the north-east city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade and another in Tours, the use of an eye.
Authorities estimate hundreds of thousands of protesters, including students, teachers and delegates from trade unions, took to the streets on Tuesday as protests sweep the country.
In Paris, tear gas filled the air, and trash cans, school desks and chairs were set alight as riot police with shields and batons clashed with some demonstrators.
The original protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on September 21 attracted little attention. Pupils had joined their teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff sent to the school, the strike ended, but by then the match had been lit. According to student leader Manès Nadel, it spread like wildfire.
“It’s an unprecedented number of schools that are now involved,” he said, adding that France’s Education Ministry had been “totally overwhelmed by the crisis.”
Despite their suburban beginnings, the protests are now drawing international attention. US President Donald Trump claimed Tuesday that “what’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration.”
“This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
Pupils at lycées in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances, and within days similar scenes were reported across the country, from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement. More than 100 high schools have been damaged since the start of the protest movement.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. One policeman was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in Alençon, a technique now prohibited by law.
The violence and the speed with which the protests have grown have taken many by surprise, but the grievances are long-standing — an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system that many students feel is no longer fit for purpose. Videos have circulated for years showing classrooms with too few desks or chairs, or students finding their classes cancelled when an absent teacher is not replaced.
A fertility spike in France in 2010 has led to a rise in the number of high school students now attending schools that have seen years of real-terms funding cuts. Secondary schools now have fewer teachers than in 2008, despite an extra 250,000 students enrolled. In the public sector, 70% of classrooms have more than 30 pupils per class.
Critics say the government’s response has been slow and tin-eared. Initially much of it was focused on the far-left LFI party and its presence at the barricades. The party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, who’s expected to do well in the country’s presidential election next spring, has repeatedly defended both the students’ right to protest and his party’s right to be there. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for a firm police response and the cost of the protest. Damage to schools in the greater Paris region alone is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.84 million).
There was an initial concession over the fees at technological high schools that had been planned for 2027 but this has now been removed from the government’s budget. “The government’s response has been irresponsible and it confirms exactly why the students are angry, because they are never heard,” said Manes. “They are responding only with repression.”
The protesters do now have the government’s full attention, especially after a spike in violence late last week, when the interior minister noted a shift from student protest to urban violence and some 2,000 people were taken into custody in a single day. On Friday, Edouard Geffray, the education minister, met with student leaders. No agreement was reached, however, and the student leaders called for a massive turnout on Tuesday immediately afterward.
France’s interior ministry estimated there were about 256,000 protesters out on the streets nationwide on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris. Meanwhile, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, one of the high school student unions involved in organizing the demonstrations, suggested a much larger turnout of 450,000 people across the country.
More than 400 people were detained in Tuesday’s protests, the ministry said.
Some students have called for fresh demonstrations on Thursday.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, speaking in the National Assembly on Tuesday, said “extreme violence has reached the gates of our high schools and it must be condemned unequivocally.”
Lecornu said 215 students and 85 education staff have been injured during the unrest, calling it “the highest number of education staff injured in decades.” He rejected accusations that the government had ordered police to repress the protests.
He also said officials must listen to the concerns and demands of students at each school.
“That is why time will be set aside starting this week, from Wednesday, to allow each leadership team to organize a session of internal democracy within its high school,” he wrote on X.
The Education Ministry has launched an online portal where students can share their concerns and ideas for improving their education.
The government’s response is being hampered by the poor state of the public finances. It is trying to pass a 2027 budget that narrows the deficit to around 5 percent of GDP, a feat that can only be achieved by painful belt-tightening. Last week France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5 percent last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook.
The unrest has fired the starting gun on what promises to be a vicious race between the far right and far left for the presidency, with much of the center floundering in the polls. For the far left, the pupils are a natural constituency. For the government, they’re a source of disorder and of spending pressure at the worst possible moment.
Historically, student protests have not gone well for French governments. The student protest of May 1968 turned into the largest strike in French history, in a country that knows a thing or two about strikes. One of its slogans was “be realistic, ask for the impossible.”
The difference now is that the students who’ve taken to the barricades once again don’t feel they are asking for much. In fact, they say they are demanding the bare minimum: an education system that allows them to learn.
CNN’s Saskya Vandoorne, Lucie Lepellec, Kate Irby and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says intelligence shows Russia is preparing massive attack
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says intelligence shows Russia is preparing massive attack
articles.content_orig:
In brief: President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Tuesday evening that new intelligence points to Russian preparations for a massive strike, urging Ukrainians to heed air raid alerts. Hours later, Ukraine’s Air Force reported three Tu-160 strategic bombers taking off, saying possible cruise missiles could enter Ukrainian airspace after 3 a.m. local time.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged Ukrainian citizens to take shelter when air raid alerts sound, citing updated intelligence reports about a massive strike planned by Moscow.
Ukrainian emergency services and the Air Force are ready to respond, Zelensky said in his evening address on Tuesday, Oct. 6, but the scale of their response depends on the air defense capabilities available to the country.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“A lot depends on our partners – every leader and every country in the world that has the defensive capabilities we need and can provide them to us,” Zelensky said, urging allies to continue supplying Kyiv as the war nears its fifth winter.
Hours later, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported that three Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers had taken off from Belaya airbase in Russia’s Siberian Irkutsk region.
In case the aircraft fire cruise missiles, the missiles could likely cross into Ukrainian airspace sometime after 3 a.m. local time, the Air Force said, urging citizens not to ignore air raid alerts and to stay in shelters.
The evening address followed an initial warning Zelensky issued on Tuesday afternoon.
He announced the warning after a coordination meeting with government officials, military commanders and emergency services. According to the president, Kyiv was also preparing countermeasures.
At that meeting, the defense minister and the Air Force commander briefed the president on how air defense assets were being distributed and how protection was organized around key facilities.
Zelensky said the government and regional authorities had also prepared additional logistics measures in response to what he called a Russian operation against Ukraine’s logistics. Deadlines were set for many of the tasks, and the most urgent ones were already underway.
Separately on Tuesday, Zelensky chaired a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief.
According to the president, electronic warfare systems neutralize a significant share of Russia’s Shahed drones, and the most effective approaches will be scaled up.
The meeting also set priorities for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones next year, with the main goal of giving Ukraine the ability to respond in kind to Russian strikes.

articles.title_orig: How Russia and the world are responding to a possible case of pneumonic plague after lab worker death
articles.title_zh: How Russia and the world are responding to a possible case of pneumonic plague after lab worker death
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The World Health Organization says a possible case of pneumonic plague in Russia presents a “very low” risk outside the country as investigators look into what caused the death from pneumonia of a lab employee there last week.
The U.N. health agency said on Tuesday that it has been in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
The case and the investigation, led by Russian officials, have revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab. WHO has not provided a definitive answer to how the pandemic began.
Here's what to know about the case and how experts are mobilizing after the woman's death:
Pneumonic plague is a form of the disease that affects the lungs
The incubation period for pneumonic plague — which means lung-based and is the most virulent form of the disease — can be as short as 24 hours, according to WHO. It’s a less common but severe form that can spread between people through respiratory particles.
If untreated, the illness can be fatal, but recovery rates are high if detected and treated in time — within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms, WHO says.
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often involving the coughing up of blood.
The more common form of plague — bubonic plague — is caused by the bite of an infected flea, and can develop into open sores filled with pus.
Pneumonia is a form of acute respiratory infection that is mostly caused by viruses or bacteria, and is spread generally through contact with infected people or from airborne droplets. WHO says pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide.
A look at what Russian officials are saying about the case
Through an international health alert system, Russian health officials on Tuesday said a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing of the deceased woman's contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests.
“Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts,” said the note from Russian authorities, which was relayed to The Associated Press by WHO.
"Based on available data, laboratory test results, and health status, medical monitoring for 100% of the contacts has now been concluded," it said. “The epidemiological situation is stable and remains under monitoring.”
The woman died at a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside the city of Irkutsk, and its mayor said the hospital was placed under quarantine. The top officials from Russia’s national public health watchdog traveled to the region on Friday.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov advised the public to follow official statements from the watchdog agency, Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumors or speculation.”
WHO has mobilized its own experts to look into the case
WHO spokesman Christian Lindmeier told a U.N. briefing on Tuesday that the institute where the woman worked “studies dangerous pathogens,” including plague in a part of Siberia where the disease "occurs naturally in wild animals.”
He said Russian officials have not yet asked for WHO experts to deploy to Russia, where authorities are "looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death.”
In recent days, WHO has brought in technical experts to its Geneva headquarters and the European regional office in Copenhagen in connection with the investigation, including specialists in high-threat pathogens.
“The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates ... the risk to be moderate-to-low for Irkutsk; a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole; and very low for the WHO European region,” Lindmeier said.
Trump and Rubio have commented on the case
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he was watching the situation with concern and that the United States would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the case.
Asked about Trump’s remarks, Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Tuesday that “it is always very good when mutual assistance is offered.” He wouldn’t elaborate further, deferring to Rospotrebnadzor.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russian authorities to share more information.
“Maybe there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” he said at a news conference in Iceland. “We’re watching it very closely and I think the whole world is watching it very closely."
“We encourage Russia to be more transparent and share more information with the world,” Rubio said, adding this has so far been “quite limited, but hopefully that will change in the next few hours and days.”
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia,” although because of modern living conditions and antibiotics, its potential was limited.
Dr. Glenn Wortmann, at the MedStar Washington Hospital Center, said the bacteria that cause plague don't “travel very far” and a person would “really need to be face-to-face” with an infected person to get pneumonic plague.
“The chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen, not with this type of bacteria, because it’s not spread easily and we have antibiotics to stop it from spreading,” he added.
Associated Press writers Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, and Matthew Lee in Reykjavik, Iceland, contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.content_orig:
Artistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris show
“It’s a good start,” Matthieu Blazy said after a Paris show that marked a year of his tenure as artistic director at Chanel . “I am happy with where we are at.”
Chanel now holds the top spot in the Lyst index of the world’s hottest brands, which tracks demand and engagement across search and social media. The privately held company announces official financial results only once a year, but figures reported by Bloomberg showed 16% growth in the first half of 2026. In Vanity Fair’s list of the world’s 50 most powerful people, published this month, Blazy is the only fashion designer to make the cut. People who don’t much care about fashion have noticed him; people who do care about fashion talk about him non-stop.
Blazy’s Chanel is about joy. Smiley and chatty in person, he enthuses about his team and the women he dresses, presenting a friendly face of Chanel that contrasts with Karl Lagerfeld’s legendary acid tongue and Coco’s controlled brutalist chic. He talks about his job like a child in a candy store, not a tortured artist: he got the idea for this stage set, a flock of 95 giant white birds suspended from the domed steel and glass ceiling of the Grand Palais in Paris, while on holiday in southern Italy with his partner, watching migrating birds fly above the Crati River.
One of Chanel’s most famous adverts of the 1990s featured Vanessa Paradis in a birdcage ; now, Chanel’s birds fly free. For the soundtrack of the show Blazy had asked Nicole Kidman to read a passage “about time, about freedom” from Virginia Woolf’s To The Lighthouse, which he had read on that Italian holiday. Fashion was “women’s homemade remedy for the dark times”, he said.
After several years when the decaffeinated aesthetic of quiet luxury dominated fashion, the new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours. A red and white embroidered jacket with a jade and turquoise skirt, plus bag and boots in navy and gold. The iconic two-tone pumps, but in zebra stripes and yellow polka dots instead of the traditional camel and black.
The same model opened and closed the show carrying Gabrielle Chanel’s very own 2.55 handbag. “Gabrielle actually had very few bags in her own life, which is something I find quite beautiful. So this bag is not broken, but it has a wonderful patina,” Blazy said.
after newsletter promotion
On his moodboard were photographs of the founder he had found in the archive: Gabrielle as a child; with Gigot, her beloved great dane; on a boat; riding a horse; in a Harlequin fancy dress costume; smiling in a bold leopard-print coat and matching hat. “It is a side of Chanel that is not known: her funny side, her joyful side. I see women as a juxtaposition of so many selves, and Chanel had this incredible layering within herself.”
The famous soft-shouldered Chanel suit came worn with nothing beneath, “like perfume” (Blazy, a student of Cocology, will not have missed the allusion to what Marilyn Monroe famously said she wore in bed: Chanel No 5). “I like the idea that when you wear it directly on the skin, it makes a fetish of the suit. A little punk Chanel,” he said. A year of fabric innovation was behind the newest versions of the suit, a smocked silk on an elasticated membrane, which “is my answer to what sporty could mean at Chanel”, Blazy said.

articles.title_orig: Lucille Lortel 2026-2027 Season Features 2 World Premieres
articles.title_zh: Lucille Lortel 2026-2027 Season Features 2 World Premieres
articles.content_orig:
The Off-Broadway company will offer new works from Benjamin Benne and Leah Nanako Winkler .
October 06, 2026 By Andrew Gans
The Lucille Lortel Theatre's 2026-2027 season includes two world premieres, a digital play reading, and more.
From November 7–December 20, 2026, Primary Stages and Lucille Lortel Theatre, in association with Jan McAdoo , will present the world premiere of Benjamin Benne's Fantasma at 59E59 Theaters. Directed by Laurie Woolery, casting and additional creative team members will be announced at a later date. The play is set on Christmas Eve as three generations of women gather in Rosie's kitchen to make chuchitos. While her granddaughters attempt to document the dish step-by-step, they discover that what's being preserved isn't just food.
In the spring, Ma-Yi Theater Company and WP Theater, in association with Lucille Lortel Theatre, will present the world premiere Leah Nanako Winkler 's You Seem Sad. Directed by May Adrales with casting to be announced, performances are scheduled for April 3–May 2, 2027, at WP Theater. The new play weaves post-WWII Nagasaki and early-2000s New York City together through the parallel journeys of Keiko—an atomic-bomb survivor rebuilding her life in 1950s Japan—and Student 1, a half-Japanese 20-something who is reckoning with her career, love, and identity in contemporary America.
A free digital reading of American Nightmare , by Lortel-commissioned playwright Hassan Abdulrazzak, is currently available for streaming through October 19. Directed by Donnacadh O’Briain, the cast of the play, set during a negotiation in a Dubai conference room, features Tom Byrne, Lanna Joffrey, Khalid Laith, and Joe Richardson with stage directions by Caden Cristiano and dramaturgy by Callan McCarthy and William Gregory . Registration is required and can be made by clicking here.
Since 2023, The Alcove at the Lortel has awarded over 40 commissions to early and mid-career playwrights. The fifth round of commissioned playwrights include Amara J. Brady, Libby Carr , Alyssa Haddad-Chin , Max Langert, Katarzyna Müller, Dhari Noel, Reynaldo Piniella , Ro Reddick , Gretchen Suárez-Peña, and Mallory Jane Weiss. These commissions may be followed by further development with dramaturgs, directors, or designers.
For additional details about the season, including offerings in the Playwright's Salon digital series and the Conversations From the Alcove web series, visit Lortel.org .

articles.title_orig: Europe’s moment of supreme confidence
articles.title_zh: Europe’s moment of supreme confidence
articles.content_orig:
As global alliances shift and economic competition intensifies, Europe is responding with deeper integration, large-scale investment and renewed confidence in its industrial and technological strengths
If there is one key takeaway from the recent Munich Security Conference, it is a message of trust and confidence in Europe. The EU is a technology, trade and industry powerhouse. Around Europe, the signs of this strength abound: off the northern coast of Poland, just beyond the horizon, 233 giant turbines – each almost as tall as the Eiffel Tower – are about to rise from the sea floor. With German rotors, foundations designed in Denmark, and cables from Poland and Greece, they will be towering symbols of European manufacturing excellence and industrial might. As the latest additions to an already vast Baltic fleet, they are creating thousands of jobs across the supply chain; and when they are operational, they will supply an additional 5.5 million households with clean energy.
Producing energy made in Europe, by Europe, for Europe, Poland’s offshore wind farms are as important strategically as they are economically. They add to a buildout of clean power that is happening across the continent from Italy in the South to Ireland and Lithuania in the North. Cables and interconnectors – enough to wrap the Earth many times over – are being laid to link the windy northern seas with the sunlit Mediterranean coastline, creating a superhighway for the age of electrons.
An investment revolution is underway Meanwhile, cutting-edge fibre-optic sensors pioneered by Dutch innovators will be watching over the seabed to protect Europe’s critical infrastructure. New constellations of satellites developed in Belgium will offer enhanced surveillance capabilities from space, alongside cutting-edge radar systems from France and Spain. And all these systems will be connected by AI-powered 6G networks developed in Finland.
These are just a few of the nearly 900 investment projects financed by the European Investment Bank Group last year alone ( see Fig 1 ). By leveraging EU budget guarantees to mobilise private investment, the EIB Group is powering the unfolding energy and technological revolutions. The transition into tomorrow’s world is already in full swing in Europe – a major development that remains overlooked amid rapid geopolitical change. In fact, the overall investment in the EU’s energy transition reached a new record in 2025, approaching €400bn – from hydropower in Austria to new railways in Czechia, and from energy efficiency upgrades by small businesses in Croatia to clean technologies deployed by heavy industries in Portugal. Just in the past year, the combined market capitalisation of European renewables companies has risen by over 50 percent. Something that many thought impossible in the near term is already happening – Europe is irreversibly weaning itself off Russian gas.
European investments in defence are increasing even more rapidly. European defence stocks have tripled in value in the past three years. Europe’s industrial production capacity now exceeds even that of the US in critical areas, including artillery shells. Europe is moving by leaps and bounds into strategic sectors and technologies such as drones.
A new venture-capital ecosystem geared toward pioneering security and defence enterprises has emerged almost overnight and essentially from scratch.
A continent reshaped by disruption We have seen a similar mobilisation before. In 2020, no one expected that a European biotech company would pioneer a vaccine against an unknown virus in a matter of months, helping the world defeat a once-in-a-century pandemic. Nor did anyone think that European leaders would launch a massive recovery and resilience programme financed by joint debt – an unprecedented show of solidarity and unity. When Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine caused a massive spike in energy prices, everyone assumed that the European economy would buckle. Instead, the eurozone’s GDP grew faster than China and the US that year.
In the face of trade warfare, intense market volatility, and shifting traditional partnerships and alliances, European companies have proven resilient, not only diversifying their trade flows but also maintaining strong growth and investment. European stock markets ended up outperforming US exchanges in 2025, rewarding investors who put their trust in our economy. Unemployment is hovering near record lows, and growth is picking up – thanks to high-performing countries such as Spain and Poland. Europe has emerged as a beacon of stability in an uncertain world.
Time and again, the EU has adapted and reinvented itself in the face of crises, leaving it well prepared to navigate a tempestuous geopolitical environment. An export powerhouse, the EU is home to world-class universities and research centres, as well as a vibrant start-up ecosystem. Opinion polls show record levels of public support for the EU and the euro, and global surveys indicate that majorities around the world see the EU as a great power on an equal footing with the US and China.
European stock markets ended up outperforming US exchanges in 2025
They are right to do so. With a $22trn economy, a vast single market of nearly a half-billion people, and plans for another wave of enlargement, Europe’s weight in the world is undeniable. It may be a different kind of superpower, one that prizes values, rules, and multilateralism over sheer might. But its power lies in its commitment to principles and willingness to back its partners and allies, as demonstrated by its status as the biggest source of financial and military assistance to Ukraine.
Europe continues to build bridges in a world of walls. It is the world’s leading trade power, residing at the centre of a vast, ever-expanding network of free-trade agreements. It is also an investment superpower that promotes shared prosperity around the world. As the biggest source of humanitarian aid and development finance, Europe funds everything from global vaccination campaigns to projects to improve water supplies in Amman and Karachi. We do so because we remain committed to the same values that brought us this far. European unification started nearly eight decades ago from the ashes of two world wars. Our parents and grandparents learned from the tragedies and mistakes of that dark era, and we can draw inspiration from their example to shape a better future for ourselves and others around the world. Ours is a society based on inclusion, equality of opportunity, intellectual freedom, peace, and the rule of law.
We know what needs to be done to preserve this way of life. We need even deeper integration, including our capital markets. We need even more large-scale investment in critical infrastructure and strategic capabilities. We need simplification to make the EU more agile and efficient. And we need more win-win partnerships and alliances to diversify our supply chains and open new markets for our goods. Momentum is building in all these areas. European leaders’ minds are focused, and we are determined to capitalise on Europe’s strengths as the world’s underappreciated superpower.

articles.title_orig: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.title_zh: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.content_orig:
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the world’s largest telescope.
Will Cushman, wcushman@wisc.edu, (563) 543-2318
Today, Francis Halzen , a University of Wisconsin–Madison professor of physics, was named the recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.
The prize was conferred for Halzen’s contributions to our understanding of the astrophysical particles known as neutrinos, produced by the universe’s most energetic events.
Watch the livestream of the press conference with Professor Halzen and leaders from UW–Madison.
“This is a celebration of a very unusual project,” says Halzen. “It is difficult to imagine that we could have pulled this off anywhere but at UW–Madison with its unique research infrastructure. The success of this project involved some luck, and I was fortunate to be at UW, where unconventional ideas can thrive and where I had the support of a remarkable community, from talented engineers at the Physical Sciences Laboratory to long-time colleagues on the faculty and supportive administrators. It is hard to imagine this project happening anywhere else.”
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory , the world’s largest — and perhaps strangest — telescope. The U.S. National Science Foundation-funded observatory is operated by an international collaboration of scientists led by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center based at UW–Madison.
Embedded in a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors to survey the universe for neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with other matter. Neutrinos provide information about the workings of black holes, galaxies and other objects in the cosmos.
“IceCube is like no other telescope in the world,” says UW–Madison interim Chancellor Eric M. Wilcots. “And there is no other scientist quite like Francis Halzen, whose idea to create a neutrino detector under almost a mile of ice has led to a remarkable multinational and multi-institutional scientific collaboration and a fundamental shift in how we think about the universe.”
Unlike the neutral neutrino, cosmic rays are charged particles whose paths cannot be traced directly back to their sources. But the powerful cosmic accelerators that produce them, like supermassive black holes, will also produce neutrinos. These so-called “ghost particles” travel nearly undisturbed from their accelerators, giving scientists an almost direct pointer to their source.
Along with observations by other telescopes, the neutrino first detected by IceCube provided the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since their discovery over 100 years ago by 1936 physics Nobel laureate Victor Hess.
In 2013, IceCube announced the first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside the solar system. The finding opened a new era of “multi-messenger astrophysics” in which not only light but particles like neutrinos and gravitational waves can provide us with information about distant cosmological events, like supermassive black holes located at the heart of galaxies. The discovery won the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award.
Four years later, in September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy in the direction of the constellation Orion. More recently, IceCube provided the first evidence of high-energy neutrino emission from an active galaxy 47 million light-years away, in 2022, and from the Milky Way, in 2023. These detections demonstrated that all three of these sources produce cosmic rays. Most recently, IceCube was successfully upgraded, marking the observatory’s first significant expansion since its completion 15 years ago.
With this award, Halzen becomes the sixth physicist connected to UW–Madison to earn the Nobel Prize. It’s the 23rd Nobel Prize tied to UW–Madison overall , in a legacy that spans medicine, chemistry, economics, engineering and physics. The last active UW–Madison faculty member to win a Nobel Prize was Howard Temin in 1975 , honored for his discovery of reverse transcriptase — a breakthrough that reshaped molecular biology and deepened understanding of diseases like Hepatitis B and HIV.
Tags: faculty awards , IceCube , Nobel Prize , physics , research
UW–Madison has been named the top volunteer-producing university since 2017.
“Best Value Schools” ranking also jumps 23 spots, placing UW–Madison 24th in the nation.
WSUM rules the airwaves thanks to creative freedom and hard work.
The project ensures that UW–Madison’s efforts at IceCube remain at the forefront of neutrino astronomy for years to come.

articles.title_orig: Indonesia Announces End to “World’s Largest Deforestation Project”
articles.title_zh: Indonesia Announces End to “World’s Largest Deforestation Project”
articles.content_orig:
Global Communications Director
The Government of Indonesia has announced that it will stop any further expansion of the Food and Energy Estates project in Papua and will shift all future development for the project for food and crops for bioenergy to degraded lands – a globally significant win for Indonesia’s nature, the climate, and local communities.
In twin announcements at the Indonesian Sustainability Forum in Jakarta, President Prabowo’s brother Hashim Djojohadikusumo, in his role as Special Envoy for Climate and Energy and the President’s Special Envoy for Multilateralism & International Trade Mari Pangestu said that Indonesia would shift both the rice and sugarcane projects to degraded land.
Mighty Earth Founder and CEO Glenn Hurowitz commented:
“President Prabowo and the Indonesian government have made a globally significant decision for people, nature and climate today by ending deforestation for its food and energy development. This decision renews Indonesia’s leadership in showing how to expand agriculture while protecting nature.”
“Mighty Earth and allies will be closely monitoring implementation, and supporting work with local communities in Papua to heal the damage that’s been done. We are hopeful about the potential of this decision to drive a continued shift to protecting and restoring nature and to sustainable agriculture.”
“This decision creates an opportunity for large-scale investments in achieving President Prabowo’s goal of restoring 12 million hectares of forest, peat, and other ecosystems. It’s a program of truly enormous significance that could provide habitat to endangered species and suck gigatons of carbon out of the atmosphere. We call on all friends of Indonesia to support this program. This decision means that Indonesia can fully achieve its potential to become a nature and climate superpower.”
01:14:00 – Rice Project Announcement by Pak Hashim, Special Envoy of the President for Energy and Climate Change.
03:19:00 – Rice and Energy Project Announcement by Ibu Mari Pangestu, Special Envoy of the President for Multilateralism & International Trade.
Excerpt from President Prabowo’s Special Envoy Hashim Djojohadikusumo speech:
“I’d like to make a major announcement. Now, because of our success in reaching rice self-sufficiency, the Government of Indonesia would like to announce especially by the Minister of Agriculture through me the Special Envoy, that the Ministry of Agriculture and the Government feels at the moment that it does not need to expand the further cultivation of rice in so-called forest areas.
The so-called 2-million-hectare food estate program is a program that we have already achieved without even planting 2 million hectares. We will embark and continue on intensification measures, using new breeds, new seeds, superior breeds of rice and soybeans to achieve that. So, I’d like to again reiterate the fact that the government sees no further need for expanding rice cultivation areas in the so-called forest areas and forest zones that were announced a few years ago…”
Excerpt from President’s Special Envoy Mari Pangestu remarks:
“I just want to repeat a very important message from Pak Hashim this morning…He basically said that because we have been committed Because we have been quite successful meaning that the 2 million hectares that were announced for food production are no longer needed. And he told me he forgot to say it and he asked me to add this message, is that, to, to have increased food and and biofuel production, moving forward, we will be using degraded land…
The missing part of that message is…We have over 12 million hectares of degraded land that can be used, for this, and the minute, and he asked me to say on his behalf that He did discuss this already with the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Forestry, and they agreed that any future production of food or biofuel production will be using degraded land, and it is part of the forestry ministry program of afforestation, reforestation, and revegetation.”
